A plucked note decays quickly, faster than on larger chordophones such as the guitar, so players often use a tremolo, striking the paired strings alternately and continuously to sustain the sound. The mandolin (Mandolin, Italian mandolino) is a plucked instrument of the lute family, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-6. It usually has four courses of double strings, eight in all, plucked with a pick and mostly tuned to the violin's pitch. The body may be bowl-back, arched-top or flat-back: the bowl-back is built of wooden staves into a bowl, the flat-back of thin boards braced inside. It is used in European classical music, the traditional music of the Peruvian Andes, American folk and bluegrass music, Irish and Brazilian folk music and Mexican estudiantina bands.

Press the strings on the frets so that they bear on the soundboard through the bridge; the soundboard vibrates and the sound comes out. A beginner can practise plucking first, then rapid alternating strokes on the same pair of strings to keep the sound going.
